title: Ebola Outbreak Explained
transcriptText:
132 deaths and 528 cases of Ebola are
already suspected in the Democratic
Republic of the Congo and Uganda.
The latest outbreak of this deadly
hemorrhagic fever was confirmed just
last Friday on May 15th with the World
Health Organization declaring it a
public health emergency of international
concern just 2 days later.
This particular outbreak of Ebola has
been caused by the Bundibugyo strain and
although there have been two outbreaks
of this strain before, there are no
specific treatments or vaccines
available for Bundibugyo Ebola.
I'm Sophia Hirshfield, a research
associate with the Global Health Policy
Center at the Center for Strategic and
International Studies. Today, I'm joined
by Michaela Simeno, fellow with the CSIS
Global Health Policy Center. Our program
has been closely tracking the rapid
progression of this outbreak. We'll have
other media and written work on the
outbreak in the coming days, but today
we're going to be sharing an update on
what we know about how the outbreak is
evolving so far. Michaela, thanks for
taking the time to chat about this
today.
>> Thanks to you, Sophia.
So, as I mentioned, this is
already a public health emergency of
international concern. Can you explain
what that means and why it's significant
that the World Health Organization has
already made this declaration?
Sure. So, the ability to declare a
public health emergency is a capability
that the World Health Organization has
under the International Health
Regulations. These are an
internationally binding tool of
international law that 196 states have
signed up to be a part of and as we can
see here, since they went into effect in
2007, we've had nine different
declarations of public health
emergencies. So, the rarity there shows
you that this is a pretty high level of
concern.
The latest for the Bundibugyo Ebola
epidemic is particularly extraordinary
because it it declared just 2 days after
the Africa CDC had first reported this
outbreak. And this emergency declaration
is meant to galvanize international
support, to raise the level of alarm,
and to signal to other partners, both
non-governmental organizations, NGOs, as
well as state partners, that there needs
to be a lot of attention on this event,
and there needs to be greater
international support paid as we move
forward.
And I wanted to talk a little bit about
the geography of this outbreak in the
Democratic Republic of the Congo,
concentrated in a place already facing
insecurity, population displacement,
population movement. What do you make of
the geography and the the geo
the geopolitical dimensions of of this
outbreak?
The first cases of this particular
Bundibugyo outbreak were reported in the
Ituri province, which is here in red in
the eastern part of the country.
And it's notable for all of the reasons
you mentioned, because there's high
insecurity in this province, and going
through some of the other provinces in
the eastern part of the country along
the border with Uganda and Rwanda.
Active conflict among rebel groups, the
M23 rebel group has taken over the city
of Goma in North Kivu.
There's a long-standing humanitarian
presence in these communities.
There's great population displacement
because of the conflict, but also
because particularly in Ituri province,
the first cases were detected in mining
communities, and so workers are
transiting back and forth in and out of
the province, and sometimes across the
border with Uganda as they're going to
work.
We're also concerned because there have
been cases reported in urban settings in
across several provinces, in Beni, in
Butembo, in Bunia.
And also in Uganda, in the capital
Kampala, there were two cases confirmed
that are not epidemiologically linked.
So, we don't know if there's other
transmission, we don't know if these
were isolated cases, but it raises the
risk of this international spread, and
so you've had Uganda put additional
screening in place. You've also had
similar measures in place in Sudan in
the northeast that borders the Ituri
province,
and Rwanda recently closed its borders.
It's important to note that from Ituri
to Kinshasa, this is an enormous
country. So, it's 1,000 km between the
two. And I mention that because of the
challenges that we had and still are
having in this outbreak with detecting
cases. And when you can't detect cases,
you can't contact trace, you can't
follow these chains of transmission, and
you can't ultimately get a handle on the
outbreak.
Most of the prior outbreaks of Ebola in
the DRC were the Zaire strain, and so
the field diagnostics are mostly
tailored to that, to what we expect to
see when it pops up.
There are much more specific uh
diagnostics that are needed to detect
the Bundibugyo strain because it's just
a species that we've only had two prior
spillovers, and most of those diagnostic
capabilities are in Kinshasa, in the
capital,
in these highly specialized labs. So,
when we had cases beginning to appear in
Ituri province at the end of April,
they were being tested for Ebola. They
weren't coming back positive because it
was testing for the wrong species, and
it was only several weeks later when
those cases tested positive in Kinshasa
that we were able to raise the level of
alarm that this was
not only Ebola, but a very unfamiliar
type of Ebola.
There's also been some concerns about
how cuts to aid could have potentially
weakened local health capabilities and
delayed the signal recognition at the
beginning of the outbreak.
Not only that, but early stages of Ebola
look very much like malaria or other
sorts of endemic diseases that are
febrile, that cause fever.
And so, when you have fewer health care
workers or less training for the health
care workers that are there because they
had were reliant on some form of
international support, that signal
recognition takes longer from the get-go
all the way through reporting when
you're able to mobilize the
international response.
And now we know that the incubation
period of Ebola can be up to 21 days.
Usually it's more like 8 to 10. So,
cases are continuing to rise and even
when we get a handle on this contact
tracing, they'll still continue to rise
from people who have been exposed from
there.
So, there's transmission at wide
geographic distances. It could have been
transmitting for about 4 weeks before we
first picked it up.
And
we're worried also about cases that have
been reported among health care workers.
Health care workers are particularly at
risk because Ebola transmits from direct
contact with the the blood or the
secretions of another person or
contaminated surfaces.
And so, those health care workers,
especially if they're in rural areas and
they don't have personal protective
equipment, are at particularly high risk
in this outbreak.
And this is just another version here
looking at some of the
huge numbers of displaced and refugee
populations that you have in the eastern
part of the country. On one hand, that
means that there are humanitarian
organizations like Médecins Sans
Frontières and the World Health
Organization that have been working with
these displaced populations for a long
time. These are also highly mobile,
highly vulnerable populations that we
need to be concerned about. Could be
much much harder to reach and and much
harder to contact trace as well. Right.
Much less formal connection with the
health care sector in many
circumstances.
So, as we previously mentioned, this is
not the first time we've had a spillover
of the Bundibugyo strain. We had a
spillover event in 2007 in Uganda, again
in 2012 in in the DRC. Um but what what
is making this outbreak different from
these prior two outbreaks of Bundibugyo
and and prior outbreaks of other strains
of Ebola as well. Obviously, we can see
there's already um
vastly higher numbers of suspected cases
and deaths in in this particular
outbreak than in those prior.
So, the DRC has a lot of experience as
does Uganda in dealing with outbreaks of
Ebola. There have been 17 outbreaks of
Ebola since the virus was first
identified in 1976 in the country. So,
that capability is there. There are
particularities about the Bundibugyo
strain and how you deal with that based
on the case fatality rate. Here, we see
ranges 30%
What's concerning, as we were discussing
around being able to identify and
diagnose and confirm cases, is that
these are our this is our suspected case
load here. So, modeling
from the tests that we have been able to
confirm and have been able to
definitively diagnose indicate that
these numbers could be much higher.
There could be up to 800 or 1,000 cases
right now. And and our our confirmed
case numbers are much lower than um
than the suspected.
Right. And so, this is
uh there's a number of factors driving
this. One is the need for these more
sensitive tests that can pick up the
Bundibugyo strain
uh that are tailored specifically to be
able to look for the strain versus just
Zaire and getting those out of these
specialized microbiology labs to the
front line to field health care workers.
The other concern is this transporting
of samples that you need to do and the
delays and so you end up having these
bottlenecks where patients are waiting
to be confirmed and waiting to be
treated. You end up having to treat
folks symptomatically and rely on astute
health care workers who are looking for
these illnesses as they pop up.
One of the things we need to be most
worried about is that you have all of
these tools in your tool kit when you're
responding to an outbreak and we don't
have the medical countermeasures that
we've relied on in the past few
outbreaks
to really get a handle on community
spread. There are vaccines that have
been developed against other strains of
Ebola, but they have not been developed
specifically for the Bundibugyo strain
and there's clinical trials that should
be getting underway to test whether some
combination of those existing vaccines
could have some cross protection in this
case against the species.
We also don't have specific diagnostics.
There are monoclonal antibody therapies
out there, but those are highly specific
to the species and strain, so there's
additional work being done to test new
cocktails that could be applicable in
this case as well as other therapies
like remdesivir that have more broad
applicability against the family of
filoviruses of which Ebola is a part and
Marburg and some of these other scary
hemorrhagic fevers.
We know that even if we do get to the
point where we have vaccines that have
proven to be
effective, it will take somewhere
between two and nine months before we
have those doses ready to deploy. So
that's a long timeline where then we're
going to be relying on traditional
public health measures going into the
community, making sure there are safe
burial practices because
deceased persons, those bodies can
remain infectious for a few days after,
so having safe and dignified burials,
having personal protective equipment for
health care workers, having them be
trained how to use that equipment, and
how to care for these really ill Ebola
patients who can be ill for quite some
time. So, it's a long period of
supportive care.
And as we've had reductions in both US
aid, as well as in aid from the United
Kingdom, these have knock-on effects on
WHO capabilities, their emergency funds
they're able to deploy, as well as these
community-level
healthcare workers who are trying to
deal with the response. So, you've had
some commitments of early funding from
the United States and others to
build Ebola treatment units and such,
but it in this early stage where the
main concern is containment, those
treatment considerations are really
important, but they won't get a handle
on the overall scope of this outbreak as
it continues to scale exponentially
here.
Well, thank you, Michaela, for taking
the time to share this data with us
today and for having this important
conversation. Our program will continue
to track this evolving outbreak, and
we're going to be posting other videos
and publications in the coming days and
weeks on our website, csis.org.
And you can also track our work on
LinkedIn at CSIS Global Health Policy
Center. A special thanks to our stellar
streaming and broadcasting team for
producing this video, and we'll see you
next time.
